items.followUp: Why does water evaporate faster when it is spread over a large surface?

rubric.why: Identifies the stronger attraction between water molecules compared with alcohol molecules.
rubric.description: Water molecules have stronger intermolecular attractions than alcohol molecules.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that water has stronger hydrogen bonding or intermolecular forces.

rubric.why: Connects stronger attractions to the higher energy needed for boiling.
rubric.description: More energy is needed to overcome these attractions, so water has a higher boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the stronger attractions to a greater energy requirement or higher boiling point.

modelAnswer: Water molecules form stronger hydrogen bonds with one another than alcohol molecules do.
More energy is therefore needed to separate the water molecules, giving water a higher boiling point.

items.followUp: Why does water have a higher boiling point than ether?

rubric.why: States the effect of increasing exposed surface area.
rubric.description: A larger surface area increases the rate of evaporation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that evaporation becomes faster when surface area increases.

rubric.why: Explains that more liquid molecules are exposed and can escape from the surface.
rubric.description: More molecules are exposed at the surface and can escape into the vapour.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining why a larger surface area speeds evaporation.

modelAnswer: Increasing the surface area of a liquid increases its rate of evaporation.
More molecules are exposed at the surface and can escape into the air.

items.followUp: Define density and state the density of water in g/cm³.

rubric.why: Gives density as mass per unit volume.
rubric.description: Density is the mass of a substance per unit volume.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition or the relationship density = mass/volume.

rubric.why: Gives the standard density of water.
rubric.description: The density of water is 1000 kg/m³, or 1 g/cm³.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either correct value with its unit.

modelAnswer: Density is the mass of a substance per unit volume.
The density of water is 1000 kg/m³ (or 1 g/cm³).

rubric.why: Identifies a defining property of liquids.
rubric.description: A liquid has a definite volume.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a liquid has a definite or fixed volume.

rubric.description: A liquid has no definite shape and takes the shape of its container; it can flow.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one correct additional property, such as taking the container's shape or flowing.

modelAnswer: A liquid has a definite volume.
A liquid has no definite shape and takes the shape of its container; it can flow.

items.followUp: Why is gold often found in nature in the uncombined state?

rubric.why: States that silver and gold have low reactivity.
rubric.description: Silver and gold are less reactive metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying their low reactivity.

rubric.why: Gives the reason for their low reactivity in terms of electron loss.
rubric.description: Their atoms do not readily lose electrons to form positive ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that they have little tendency to lose electrons or form ions.

modelAnswer: Silver and gold are less reactive metals.
Their atoms do not readily lose electrons to form positive ions.

items.followUp: Distinguish between a saturated and an unsaturated solution.

rubric.why: Defines a saturated solution by the maximum amount of dissolved solute at a particular temperature.
rubric.description: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at a given temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct defining condition for a saturated solution.

rubric.why: Distinguishes an unsaturated solution by its ability to dissolve more solute.
rubric.description: An unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute at that temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that more solute can still dissolve.

modelAnswer: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a particular temperature.
An unsaturated solution contains less than this amount and can dissolve more solute at that temperature.

items.followUp: Give two differences between a true solution and a suspension.

rubric.why: Gives the difference in whether particles settle on standing.
rubric.description: Colloidal particles do not settle on standing, whereas suspension particles settle.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct settling distinction.

rubric.why: Gives the difference in separation by filtration.
rubric.description: Colloidal particles pass through ordinary filter paper, whereas suspension particles can be separated by filtration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct filtration distinction.

modelAnswer: Colloidal particles do not settle on standing, whereas particles in a suspension settle.
Colloidal particles pass through ordinary filter paper, whereas suspension particles can be separated by filtration.

items.followUp: Describe how Bohr's model explains the line spectrum of hydrogen.

rubric.why: Recognises Rutherford's central, positively charged nucleus.
rubric.description: Rutherford proposed a small, dense, positively charged nucleus at the centre of the atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the nucleus's positive charge and central position or its small, dense nature.

rubric.why: Includes the main implication of Rutherford's model about the atom's structure.
rubric.description: Most of the atom is empty space, with electrons around the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that most of the atom is empty space or that electrons surround the nucleus.

rubric.why: Identifies Bohr's allowed electron orbits or energy levels.
rubric.description: Bohr proposed that electrons move in fixed orbits or shells with definite energies.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the fixed-orbit or fixed-energy-level idea.

rubric.why: States that electrons in allowed orbits do not continuously lose energy.
rubric.description: Electrons do not radiate energy while they remain in an allowed orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electrons do not lose or radiate energy in these orbits.

rubric.why: States how Bohr's model accounts for energy changes or a limitation resolved by the model.
rubric.description: Electrons absorb or emit definite amounts of energy when they change levels; this explains atomic stability and the hydrogen line spectrum, unlike Rutherford's model.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing energy absorption or emission during a transition, or for stating that Bohr's model explains stability or the hydrogen line spectrum.

modelAnswer: Rutherford proposed that an atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus containing most of its mass.
Electrons revolve around the nucleus, and most of the atom is empty space.
Rutherford's model could not explain why revolving electrons do not lose energy and fall into the nucleus, or explain atomic line spectra.
Bohr proposed that electrons can revolve only in certain fixed orbits or shells, each with a definite energy.
Electrons do not radiate energy while they remain in these allowed orbits.
An electron absorbs or emits a definite amount of energy when it jumps between energy levels; this explains atomic stability and the hydrogen line spectrum.
